name: Bianca Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do new connections on the south side of the city, where they're building housing estates as fast as they can sell them. So I'm the one who runs the cable from the street to a new house, fits the cut-out, which is the big fuse where the power comes in, and gets it ready for the meter. Some weeks it's forty houses on one estate, all the same, and you could do them blindfold. Other weeks it's an old farmhouse that's finally getting a proper supply.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the families on moving day, when they see the lights come on in their new kitchen. I've done that for a lot of young couples, and I always think of when David and I got our first place. What wears me out is the builders. They dig trenches in the wrong place and then ring us in a panic. I use the AI thing now and then, mostly to help David word his invoices for the plumbing business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper and nothing more, and I'd be glad of it. At work I'd say the houses still need wiring and that's that. I don't post much online, just photos of the grandchildren-to-be when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I finish at sixty-two as planned. David's business keeps going, the rental flat keeps paying, and Grace can do her apprenticeship without worrying. It's the best of the five for our family, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd carry on with the connections, keep putting a bit aside each month, and help David with his paperwork. I'd tell Grace to go ahead with the electrical apprenticeship she's been thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, like a Sunday with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You help David with invoices using AI. Would you keep doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It turns my rough notes into something polite. David's customers pay faster now. That's about as much as I need from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that mean for Grace's choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it easy. She's twenty-four and torn between a university course in business and an electrical apprenticeship. I've always said a trade is a good, honest living. In this one, she'd take the apprenticeship and I'd be proud.

S0.say: It's a useful helper and nothing more, and I'd be glad of it. The houses still need wiring, and that's that.
S0.think: It means I finish at sixty-two as planned, David's business keeps going and the rental flat keeps paying. It's the best of the five for our family, really.
S0.do: Keeps working on new connections and saving a bit each month, and keeps helping her husband with his paperwork. Encourages her daughter to go ahead with an electrical apprenticeship.
S0.quote: It turns my rough notes into something polite. David's customers pay faster now.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca thinks about the whole household: her job, her husband's plumbing business, the rental flat and her daughter's choice. She uses AI modestly and sees no threat here. Her pride in trades runs through everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, like it always is, and people with a good trade will be all right. I'd say it at work and at church. You adapt, you don't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's fine for my last few years. But I'd start to wonder about Grace. If lots of jobs shift around, is an apprenticeship still the safe bet I've always said it is? I'd want to be sure before I push her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which jobs actually shrink before I said anything to Grace either way. At work I'd learn whatever new planning or metering software they gave us once the others had tried it. I'd talk with David about whether he needs to change anything in the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it'd be on my mind at the kettle in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I still think a trade is good, but to pick one that needs a person on the spot, like electrical work, not one that's all forms. And I'd tell her to learn the computer side too, so she isn't caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new tools change your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the scheduling and the paperwork, telling us which estate to go to and logging the job. Fine by me, if it means fewer phone calls from builders. Hands on the cable stays mine.

S1.say: It's change, like it always is, and people with a good trade will be all right. You adapt, you don't complain.
S1.think: I think my job's fine for my last few years, but I'd start to wonder about Grace. Is an apprenticeship still the safe bet I've always said it is?
S1.do: Waits to see which jobs actually shrink before advising her daughter, and learns new scheduling or metering software once colleagues have tried it. Talks with her husband about any changes his business might need.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the worry on her mind each morning but not keeping her up.
S1.quote: Not losing sleep, but it'd be on my mind at the kettle in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: Her public message is about adapting without complaint, but privately she questions the advice she's always given her daughter. She adopts tools once others have proven them. Her worry centres on family decisions rather than her own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, and families need to pull together. I wouldn't say the government should fix it, because I don't think they can. I'd say it at work and to the neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. If robots can wire houses in 2028, my job's done when I'm sixty. That's fine for money, we've got the rental flat and the savings. But David's business is hands-on too, and Grace would be starting an apprenticeship for a job that might not be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about early retirement straight away and take it if it's decent. I'd sit down with David and talk about selling the plumbing business while it's still worth something. I'd tell Grace to hold off on the apprenticeship and keep her current job for now, and we'd put more aside each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a call from the builder saying they've hit something and they don't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to David's plumbing business in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard one. He's built it for twenty years. Three vans and two lads working for him. If machines can do it cheaper in two years, he either sells now or watches it go to nothing. I don't think he'd want to hear that from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I don't know, which I hate saying. I've always had an answer for her. I'd tell her to wait, keep her job, and we'll help her when it's clearer.

S2.say: We need to look after our own, and families need to pull together. I don't think the government can fix it, so I wouldn't say they should.
S2.think: I'd be worried. My job would end when I'm sixty, which is fine for money, but David's business is hands-on too and Grace would be training for a job that might not be there.
S2.do: Asks about early retirement straight away and takes it if the terms are decent. Talks with her husband about selling his plumbing business while it still has value, tells her daughter to hold off the apprenticeship, and saves more each month.
S2.feel: Anxious, like hearing a builder has hit something underground and nobody knows what.
S2.quote: I'd tell her I don't know, which I hate saying. I've always had an answer for her.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline threatens her family's two trades at once, which is what makes her anxious. She stresses family self-reliance over government. Admitting she has no answer for her daughter was hard for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's be sensible and make plans as families. I'd say the companies should keep training apprentices as long as there's work. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm retired anyway. I think it's mostly about David and Grace again. Five years is enough to plan, so I'd be less worried than with the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-two as planned. I'd help David plan a sale over three or four years, not in a rush. I'd tell Grace to do a shorter course, maybe a year in electrical installation, and keep her options open. We might buy a second small rental flat with some of the savings, because people still need somewhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's the kind of worry you can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let your family do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it properly. Sell David's business at the right moment, not in a fire sale. Let Grace see which way things go before she commits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the business in the fast one. Would you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but in his own time. He'd want to hand it to one of his lads, Rafael, who's been with him ten years. Five years gives him time to do that properly.

S3.say: We've got time, so let's be sensible and make plans as families. Companies should keep training apprentices as long as there's work.
S3.think: By 2031 I'm retired anyway, so it's mostly about David and Grace. Five years is enough to plan, so I'd be less worried than with the fast one.
S3.do: Works to sixty-two as planned and helps her husband plan a sale or handover of his business over three or four years. Steers her daughter towards a shorter course and considers buying a second small rental flat with savings.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with a worry she can plan around.
S3.quote: He'd want to hand it to one of his lads, Rafael, who's been with him ten years.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns panic into planning for her family's assets and choices. She thinks in property and handovers, which fits her traditional, family-first outlook. Her loyalty extends to her husband's long-serving worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for families who plan ahead. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and keep learning. And I'd say people shouldn't expect someone else to sort it out for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm long retired by then. It's David's business and Grace's future, and ten years is enough for both. I'm not too worried, but I would keep half an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different for me: connections until sixty-two, then retire. David would carry on and hand over to Rafael in his own time. We'd keep the rental flat and maybe add the second one, so we're not relying on anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just a little. It's far off, but it's still our family's trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired, probably minding grandchildren. Doing the books for David, if he hasn't sold yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go for the apprenticeship, but learn the robots too. If they're going to wire houses one day, someone needs to know how to fix them, and it might as well be a girl who knows the cable.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for families who plan ahead. Learn a trade and keep learning, and don't expect someone else to sort it out for you.
S4.think: I'm long retired by then, and ten years is enough for David's business and Grace's future. I'm not too worried, but I'd keep half an eye on it.
S4.do: Keeps doing connections until sixty-two, then retires as planned. Supports her husband handing his business to his worker in his own time, and keeps the rental flat while considering a second one.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, because her family's trades are still in the path of it.
S4.quote: If they're going to wire houses one day, someone needs to know how to fix them, and it might as well be a girl who knows the cable.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives her the confidence to back the apprenticeship again, with a twist. Her family-first outlook stays consistent throughout. She relies on property and her own planning rather than outside help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because it hits me, David's business and Grace's plans all at once. What would help is the companies being honest about what's coming, and keeping apprenticeships going for as long as there's real work to train for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young couples moving in. Every one of those houses has a family who needs a job to pay for it. I think about that when I'm connecting them. Who's going to pay those mortgages if the jobs go?

headlineQuote: Every one of those houses has a family who needs a job to pay for it.
portrait: Bianca Chen is a 58-year-old lineworker who connects new houses to the grid on the city's fast-growing south side and loves seeing the lights come on for young couples. She uses AI now and then, mostly to polish her husband David's plumbing invoices, and adopts new tools once colleagues have tried them. She is secure herself, with savings and a rental flat, so her worries centre on David's business and her daughter Grace's choice of an apprenticeship. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious enough to retire early and talk David into selling, while more time lets the family plan calmly. She believes in trades, family and planning ahead, not waiting for government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit her own job, her husband's plumbing business and her daughter's plans at once.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being honest about what's coming and keeping apprenticeships going for as long as there's real work to train for.
